facts.fact_text: On 31 January 2009, the applicant and six other people decided to hold a flash mob in front of the Office of the Russian Government in Moscow.
The applicant and six other people arrived at the Office of the Russian Government in Moscow at around 1 p.m. on 31 January 2009.
The applicant and six other people positioned themselves at Gorbatyy Bridge on 31 January 2009.
Each participant in the flash mob held a blank sheet of paper.
Each participant in the flash mob had their mouth covered with adhesive tape.
At 1.20 p.m. on 31 January 2009, the police ordered the group at Gorbatyy Bridge to disperse.
The applicant was taken to Presnenskiy police station.

The applicant was charged under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences (breaches of the established procedure for the organisation or conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets).

On 11 March 2009, the justice of the peace of the 378th circuit of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow convicted the applicant of the administrative offence under Article 20.2 § 2 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The justice of the peace of the 378th circuit of the Presnenskiy District of Moscow sentenced the applicant to a fine of 1,000 Russian roubles (approximately 22 euros).

The basis for the charge against the applicant was that the requirement of prior notification under the Federal Law on Gatherings, Meetings, Demonstrations, Processions and Pickets, no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004 (the Public Events Act), had not been respected.

Section 2(1) of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004) defined a 'public event' as an open, peaceful event accessible to all, organised at the initiative of citizens of the Russian Federation, political parties, other public associations, or religious associations.

Section 2(1) of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004) provided that a public event must have the aims of expressing or developing opinions freely and voicing demands on issues related to political, economic, social or cultural life in the country, and issues related to foreign policy.

Section 2(6) of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004) defined a static demonstration as a form of public expression of opinion that does not involve movement or the use of loudspeaker equipment.

In accordance with sections 5(4)(1) and 7(1)(3) of the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004), notification in respect of a static demonstration involving several persons must be submitted no later than three days before the intended static demonstration.
Under the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004), no notification was required for gatherings (собрание).
Under the Public Events Act (Federal Law no. FZ-54 of 19 June 2004), no notification was required for static demonstrations involving one person.
A summary of the relevant domestic law and practice can be found in Kasparov and Others v. Russia (no. 21613/07, § 35, 3 October 2013).
A summary of the relevant domestic law and practice can be found in Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia (no. 76204/11, §§ 43-44, 4 December 2014).
A summary of the relevant domestic law and practice can be found in Novikova and Others v. Russia (nos. 25501/07 and 4 others, §§ 67-69, 26 April 2016).
A summary of the relevant domestic law and practice can be found in Lashmankin and Others v. Russia (nos. 57818/09 and 14 others, §§ 216-312, 7 February 2017).
